input: Sampling is a crucial step in the characterisation of gas emissions, because the quality of any subsequent analysis depends entirely on how well the sample represents the stream from which it was taken. It is important to note that a gas emission is rarely uniform: its composition can vary both across the duct and over time, and these variations must be taken into account if meaningful results are to be obtained. Samples should therefore be taken at a location where the stream is thoroughly mixed, rather than immediately downstream of bends or junctions where the flow may be stratified into layers of differing composition. In larger ducts, it is also advisable to draw the sample across the whole cross-section instead of relying on a single point close to the wall, since the gas near the wall may not reflect the composition of the bulk flow. Furthermore, a single sample should normally be built up from a number of increments, with each increment consisting of a small portion of gas drawn at a different time and the increments subsequently combined. This approach ensures that fluctuations in the emission over the sampling period are properly captured, including fluctuations associated with cyclical features of the process itself. By contrast, a single grab sample, taken at one point and at one moment, can be highly misleading: it may coincide with a temporary lull or a temporary peak, and there is no way of knowing from the result alone which has occurred. Overall, careful attention to the sampling location, the sampling pattern and the number of increments is essential if the final result is to provide a reliable picture of the emission as a whole.
target:
Sample a gas emission so that the laboratory result describes the emission, not the moment and the point at which the sample happened to be taken. A representative sample has the composition the whole stream has over the sampling period, averaged in the same proportions. Every choice in the sampling plan defends that average, and a result obtained from an unrepresentative sample cannot be repaired by careful analysis afterwards.

Take the sample where the stream is mixed. Gas leaving a bend, a junction or a partial obstruction travels in layers that differ in composition, and a probe placed in one layer draws from that layer only. A sampling plane in a straight run, downstream of the disturbance, lets the layers merge before the probe. Where the duct is wide, draw across the section rather than at a single point near the wall: the wall layer moves slowly and can differ from the core of the stream, and a wall sample reads the wall layer as if it were the stream.

Build one sample from several increments. An increment is a small portion drawn at one time; increments taken at intervals across the period and combined give a sample that follows the stream as its composition drifts. A process that cycles — a batch discharge, a firing pattern, a cleaning step — changes the emission on its own period, and increments spread over the whole cycle capture the high and the low parts of it. Record the process state alongside each increment, so that a result can later be read against the operation that produced it.

A single grab sample has neither defence. A grab sample is drawn at one point at one moment, and it reports that point and that moment faithfully. Read as the emission, it misleads in whichever direction the moment was unrepresentative: a lull understates the emission, a peak overstates it, and nothing in the result shows which has happened. Sampling effort belongs in the plane, the traverse and the increments, because the analysis that follows can only measure the sample it receives.
